Temperature difference calculatorCalculate cooling split or furnace temperature rise without leaving the app. Offline
AC TEMPERATURE DIFFERENTIAL — REFERENCE GUIDE
Follow the four field steps, then use the calculator. The guide is for quick reference and does not create duplicate inspection records.
1Run the AC for at least 15 minutes
Start the air-conditioning system and allow it to operate continuously for a minimum of 15 minutes before measuring the temperature differential.
2Measure return air at the filter housing
Go to the HVAC filter housing. Remove the filter only as necessary to obtain the return-air temperature at the filter housing, then record the reading in the calculator below.
3Restore the filter before continuing
Reinstall the filter correctly and close the filter housing. Return the system to its normal operating configuration. Do not leave the filter removed while measuring supply air.
4Measure supply air and calculate
Measure supply-air temperature at the first suitable supply register. Enter both readings below; the app calculates return minus supply and gives the configured field-screen interpretation.

Use representative locations, one verified thermometer, and the required run time. Cooling difference is a field screen—not a refrigerant or capacity diagnosis. Heating rise must be compared with the equipment nameplate range.

Well inspection & yield test timerStart once, keep working, and complete the record when the timed test is finished. Not started

Use only for a contracted well inspection/yield test. Set up the equipment safely, confirm no water is being used elsewhere, then start the timer. This is a practical functional/yield test—not a hydrogeological drawdown or recovery test.

WELL TEST COMPLETE

The well test has reached the required test duration.

1Inform client and occupants before testingEstablish the no-water-use rule before starting.Pending
  • Speak with the client and every occupant, contractor, agent, or other person present before beginning.
  • Advise everyone that no water may be used anywhere on the property for the full 100-minute test.
  • This includes toilets, sinks, showers, bathtubs, washing machines, dishwashers, exterior faucets, and every other water-using fixture or appliance.
  • Confirm that everyone understands before starting.
2Identify water discharge locationSelect a safe spigot and discharge route.Pending
  • Locate an operational exterior hose bib/spigot suitable for testing.
  • If a suitable spigot is available at the well equipment, determine whether the discharge hose can be routed safely outside.
  • Confirm the discharge will not cause flooding, erosion, water intrusion, or another unsafe condition.
3Locate and inspect well equipmentDocument the pressure tank, plumbing, and visible condition.Pending
  • Locate the accessible well equipment in the basement, crawlspace, utility room, well house, well pit, or other location.
  • Photograph the pressure tank and its manufacturer label.
  • Record the pressure tank manufacturer, model, and capacity where available.
  • Identify the visible plumbing material and check the tank, piping, fittings, and related equipment for leakage, corrosion, damage, or abnormal conditions.
4Inspect pressure controlsRecord switch range, actual pressures, and gauge response.Pending
  • Locate the pressure switch and pressure gauge.
  • Identify the pressure-switch operating range where possible, such as 20/40, 30/50, or 40/60 PSI.
  • Photograph the pressure switch and record its setting.
  • Record actual pump cut-in and cut-out pressures and confirm the gauge responds as pressure changes.
  • Document abnormal pressure fluctuation or rapid cycling.
5Set up pump amperage monitoringPosition the clamp meter safely on one energized conductor.Pending
  • Set the clamp meter to the appropriate AC amperage setting.
  • Clamp around one individual energized conductor supplying the well pump.
  • Position the meter so running amperage can be observed safely during testing.
  • Avoid contact with exposed energized electrical components.
6Set up yield-test equipmentConnect, route, photograph, and record the initial totalizer.Pending
  • Connect the well-yield equipment to the selected spigot and route the discharge hose safely outside.
  • Confirm all connections are secure.
  • Photograph the totalizing/yield meter before starting and record the initial reading.
  • Confirm again that no water is being used anywhere on the property.
7Begin the 100-minute testOpen the spigot, start the timer, and record initial flow.Pending
  • Fully open the test spigot and immediately start the 100-minute timer.
  • Confirm water is flowing through the flow meter.
  • Photograph the operating flow meter and record the initial flow rate in GPM.
8Record pump operationCapture cut-in, amperage, and operating behavior.Pending
  • Observe pressure falling until the pressure switch activates the pump and record cut-in pressure.
  • Once the pump is operating steadily, record running amperage and photograph the reading.
  • Observe for excessive cycling, pressure fluctuation, vibration, unusual noise, air, bubbles, or other abnormal operation.
9Monitor during the testQuick checks at approximately 15-minute intervals.Pending
  • At each interval check flow rate, pump amperage, system pressure, cycling, and overall operation.
  • Observe discharged water for air, bubbles, sediment, discoloration, or loss of flow.
  • Record significant changes and remain alert for unauthorized water use inside the property.
15 minutes
30 minutes
45 minutes
60 minutes
75 minutes
90 minutes
10Stop the test if necessaryProtect the pump and document every early termination.Pending
  • Terminate early if flow deteriorates significantly or reaches zero, amperage changes substantially, rapid cycling begins, significant air enters the supply, abnormal pump noise develops, or leakage/another unsafe condition occurs.
  • If stopped, document the stop time, completed duration, reason, and observed conditions.
11Complete the 100-minute testStop flow, record final totalizer, and observe recovery.Pending
  • At 100 minutes, turn off the test spigot.
  • Photograph and record the final totalizer reading.
  • Observe pressure recovery and confirm the switch reaches expected cut-out pressure and shuts the pump off normally.
  • Record abnormal recovery, cycling, or pressure behavior.
12Calculate total well yieldFinal minus initial; total gallons divided by 100 minutes.Pending
  • Total gallons produced = final totalizer reading minus initial totalizer reading.
  • Average GPM = total gallons produced divided by 100 minutes.
  • Record the initial reading, final reading, total gallons, and average GPM.
Total gallons produced—
Average yield—

Enter the initial and final totalizer readings. Average GPM is calculated only for a completed 100-minute test.

13Exterior wellhead inspectionPhotograph and inspect the accessible casing, cap, and grade.Pending
  • Locate the accessible well casing/wellhead and photograph it.
  • Check the visible casing for damage or deterioration.
  • Check the cap for damage, looseness, openings, or other contamination pathways.
  • Observe surrounding grade and confirm the wellhead is not in an obvious low area where surface water collects.
  • Document visible deficiencies.
14Final well inspection documentationReview the complete functional/yield inspection record.Pending
  • Confirm the record includes available tank photos/details, plumbing material, pressure-switch setting, actual cut-in/cut-out, running amperage, initial flow, interval observations, initial/final totalizer, total gallons, average GPM, and wellhead/casing/cap condition.
  • Document pressure fluctuations, rapid cycling, air/bubbles, sediment/discoloration, loss of flow, abnormal pump operation, and any early termination.
  • State the overall functional assessment observed during this inspection without presenting the test as a hydrogeological analysis.
Mold air samplingFollow the client concern, investigation, two indoor samples, and outdoor control in the correct field order. Not started

Three standard air samples: 15 LPM × 5 minutes = 75 liters per sample. Indoor Sample #1 normally follows the client’s primary concern. Indoor Sample #2 is selected from the inspector’s findings—never automatically assigned to the basement.

Sampling methods vary depending on the material. Minimize disturbance, control dust, document the location thoroughly, and obtain a representative sample using the least destructive practical method.

Do not automatically use the flooring/tape method for insulation, vermiculite, siding, trim, or other materials. Follow the applicable material-specific guidance.

Training record boundary: this checklist guides MPI practice and coaching. It does not issue or approve InterNACHI badges, replace the company competency sign-off, or authorize ancillary work.

01 Before/After photo recordsProperty protection · 6-minute refresher Complete

Company standard

  1. Take the Before photo before changing a thermostat, operating control, removing a cover, or opening an access component.
  2. Complete only authorized inspection procedures and stop when continued work could cause damage or create an unsafe condition.
  3. Restore the component to its original safe condition unless a safety concern requires a different action.
  4. Take the After photo from an angle that clearly shows the restored setting, cover, control, or access component.
  5. Use the damaged-item notice when the item cannot be safely restored or damage is found.
When should the Before photo be taken?
02 Cooling temperature differentialHVAC field screening · 8-minute refresher Complete

Key sequence

  1. Confirm outdoor conditions and manufacturer limits allow operation.
  2. Photograph the thermostat before changing it and inspect the visible equipment for unsafe conditions.
  3. Operate with normal controls and allow at least 15 minutes of run time when practical.
  4. Use the same verified thermometer at a representative central return and nearby supply.
  5. Record both readings, calculate return minus supply, report the actual result, and restore the thermostat.

Field screen: Approximately 14–22°F is the usual range under typical conditions. Do not diagnose refrigerant charge or system capacity from the differential alone.

What should an out-of-range result produce?
03 MPI report-writing standardObservation · Implication · Recommendation Complete

Build each defect in three parts

  1. Observation: State the component, exact visible condition, location, extent, and test result supported by the inspection evidence.
  2. Implication: Explain the likely consequence of that specific condition without claiming a concealed cause or unsupported diagnosis.
  3. Recommendation: State who should act, what they should evaluate or correct, and when action is appropriate.
  4. Use a condition-specific title such as “Toilet – Runs Continuously,” not a generic title such as “Damaged.”
  5. Never write “as described in field notes,” and never add facts that were not observed.
Which title follows the MPI standard?
04 Safe-stop and authorizationSafety boundary · 5-minute refresher Complete

Stop the affected procedure when:

  • Continued work could injure a person, damage property, or worsen a hazardous condition.
  • The task is outside the inspector’s documented training or authorization.
  • Equipment is shut down, tagged, disconnected, winterized, visibly damaged, or does not respond to normal controls.
  • Access, weather, animals, contamination, electrical conditions, or structural instability create unreasonable risk.

Move to a safe position, photograph from a safe distance when practical, notify the responsible party when warranted, and write a specific defect or limitation.

What overrides the safe-stop rule?
05 Final departure checkCloseout routine · 7-minute refresher Complete

Before leaving the property

  1. Restore and photograph thermostats, HVAC covers, electrical covers, appliances, fireplace controls, and access panels.
  2. Confirm faucets and showers are off, refrigerator/freezer doors are closed, and wet areas were rechecked for leakage.
  3. Reset tested GFCIs and leave breakers, disconnects, and shutoffs as found.
  4. Close windows, doors, garage doors, attic/crawlspace accesses, and turn lights off as appropriate.
  5. Secure keys and lockbox; account for every tool, ladder, meter, cover screw, and piece of PPE.
  6. Communicate urgent hazards and confirm the inspection report is synchronized.
What should happen if an access cover cannot be restored?
06 Electrical device testingRepresentative outlets · GFCI/AFCI · restoration Complete

Test, record, and restore

  1. Visually inspect the receptacle, cover, wiring condition, and surrounding area before using a tester.
  2. Test a representative number of readily accessible receptacles and record the exact location and displayed condition.
  3. Use the installed test control or an approved device for GFCI testing, then reset and confirm that power was restored.
  4. Test AFCI protection only when company policy and the equipment instructions permit it. Do not repeatedly reset a device that trips again.
  5. Do not remove receptacles, probe energized wiring, or perform electrical repairs during the inspection.

Source: MPI Field SOP 9.2 — representative devices and protective-device testing.

What belongs in the field record after a device test?
07 Water-heater safety boundariesIdentification · combustion · TPR valve Complete

Observe without creating a hazard

  1. Photograph the data plate and record the fuel or energy source, capacity, approximate age, and visible condition.
  2. Inspect accessible tank surfaces, connections, drain valve, pan, nearby materials, and evidence of leakage or corrosion.
  3. For fuel-fired equipment, inspect accessible venting and combustion-air conditions. Do not light a pilot or place equipment into service.
  4. Confirm the temperature-and-pressure relief valve and discharge piping are present and visibly configured; never operate the valve.
  5. Record the delivered hot-water response and ambient carbon-monoxide result when the SOP requires it.

Source: MPI Field SOP 8.4 — water heaters and hot-water sources.

How is the TPR valve evaluated during the inspection?
08 Appliance primary-function checkOperate safely · remain present · close out Complete

Use only the approved primary function

  1. Confirm the appliance is included in the inspection scope and inspect it before operation.
  2. Do not energize equipment that is tagged, disconnected, shut down, visibly unsafe, leaking, or otherwise unsuitable for testing.
  3. Operate only the approved primary function using normal controls and remain present while it runs.
  4. Stop for smoke, a gas odor, a burning odor, leakage, abnormal noise, movement, arcing, or any worsening condition.
  5. Return controls to the original position, close doors, and recheck the surrounding area for leakage or damage.

Source: MPI Field SOP 7.4 — installed appliances.

What should happen when an appliance begins leaking during the test?
09 Attic access and contaminationEntry decision · safe viewing · closeout Complete

Choose the safest inspection method

  1. Assess the ladder setup, access opening, temperature, electrical hazards, animals, structural support, and contamination before entry.
  2. Select the appropriate method: full entry, observation from the opening, or remote viewing.
  3. Never step where positive structural support is not visible and confirmed.
  4. Do not disturb suspected vermiculite, animal waste, damaged asbestos-containing material, or other unsafe contamination.
  5. Document the access method and limitation, then restore and photograph the hatch or access cover.

Source: MPI Field SOP 11.4 — attic areas.

What is the correct response when safe attic entry is not available?
10 Garage-door operator safetyClear path · approved test · restore Complete

Keep people clear of the moving door

  1. Inspect accessible panels, tracks, rollers, supports, cables, springs, and the operator from a safe distance.
  2. Keep the door path clear and operate it from the wall control with an unobstructed view.
  3. Check photoelectric protection with an approved non-contact method; never use a person as the obstruction.
  4. Do not perform a force-reversal test unless company policy and manufacturer instructions specifically authorize it.
  5. Do not touch or adjust springs, cables, or high-tension components. Restore the door to its original position.

Source: MPI Field SOP 12.2 — garage vehicle doors and operators.

How should the photoelectric protection be checked?
11 Electrical panel cover boundaryAuthorization · hazard assessment · restoration Complete

Cover removal is never automatic

  1. Only an inspector with documented MPI electrical-safety training and authorization may remove an energized dead front; a trainee acts only under the required direct supervision.
  2. Before touching the cover, confirm dry stable footing, working clearance, lighting, enclosure stability, suitable fasteners, and company-authorized tools and PPE.
  3. Do not remove the cover when moisture, severe corrosion, scorching, arcing, buzzing, abnormal heat, loose parts, damaged equipment, or another unsafe condition is present.
  4. Maintain control of the cover and every screw. Never probe, tighten, reset, or disturb energized components or conductors.
  5. Reinstall and secure the dead front immediately, account for every fastener, and take the required restored-condition photograph.

Source: MPI Field SOP 2.5 and 9.3 — electrical panel covers.

What should happen when abnormal heat and buzzing are present at the panel?
12 Ambient CO screening and responseInstrument readiness · trends · safe escalation Complete

Screen, record, and escalate without diagnosing

  1. Confirm the approved meter identity, battery, sensor/service status, calibration status, and no-fault condition.
  2. Establish zero only in reasonably carbon-monoxide-free outdoor air, then record the initial indoor background.
  3. Remain present while fuel-fired equipment operates normally and observe current, peak, and rising readings at the MPI measurement location.
  4. Follow the MPI action level and emergency procedure for a concerning, rapidly increasing, or alarm-level result, symptoms, or a building alarm. Move people to safety before documentation.
  5. Record the actual reading, location, operating conditions, instrument, and response. Do not diagnose combustion equipment from an ambient screen.

Source: MPI Field SOP 3.6 and 10.4 — ambient carbon-monoxide screening.

What has priority when an alarm-level reading or possible symptoms occur?
13 Roof and ladder access decisionSafest method · setup · limitation Complete

The safest effective method controls

  1. Inspect the ladder rails, rungs, feet, locks, strap, labels, and cleanliness before initial use; tag and remove a damaged ladder from service.
  2. Set the correct ladder on firm level footing, control doors and traffic, keep clear of conductors, and confirm every lock before climbing.
  3. Assess roof slope, material, access, weather, surface condition, edges, conductors, and the inspector’s current authorization.
  4. Roof walking is optional. Use ground views, eaves, windows, ladder views, binoculars, pole camera, or an authorized drone whenever that is safer.
  5. Record the method used, best alternate views obtained, and every area that remained unobservable.

Source: MPI Field SOP 2.3, 2.4, and 6.3 — ladders and roof access.

What is required when the roof cannot be walked safely?
14 Water sampling and chain of custodyOrdered package · clean collection · delivery Complete

The order and current laboratory instructions control

  1. Confirm the exact ordered MPI package, sample location, inspector authorization, laboratory, bottle set, preservatives, holding time, and current chain-of-custody form.
  2. Match only the ordered package and its listed parameters on the COC; do not add or omit analyses from memory.
  3. Use clean gloves and the approved collection procedure. Do not touch bottle or cap interiors, rinse a preserved bottle, or substitute a container.
  4. Label every bottle immediately and reconcile sample ID, source, collection date/time, collector, requested analyses, and preservation/cooling.
  5. Complete custody signatures and deliver within the required temperature and holding-time conditions. Report any deviation rather than concealing it.

Source: MPI water-test parameters / COC guide and current laboratory instructions.

What determines which analyses are marked on the COC?
15 Sewer scope operating boundaryApproved access · controlled advance · restoration Complete

Protect the property and the equipment

  1. Confirm the service is ordered, the inspector is authorized, and the cleanout/access arrangement is safe and approved before opening anything.
  2. Inspect the camera head, spring, seal, skid, cable, reel, monitor, battery, recording, distance counter, and property-protection setup.
  3. Create a clear access/location record, then advance the cable with controlled hand pressure while recording continuously.
  4. Never force resistance or a bend likely to trap or damage the camera. Stop at the agreed endpoint or first condition that cannot be passed safely.
  5. Withdraw steadily, contain contamination, clean/disinfect authorized components, keep the control box dry, verify the media, and restore the cleanout.

Source: MPI Sewer Scope field procedure and company tool guide.

What should the inspector do when the camera meets firm resistance?
16 Mold / IAQ sampling controlSampling plan · media identity · custody Complete

Collect the authorized sample—do not improvise

  1. Confirm the contracted scope, approved sampling plan, inspector authorization, current lab COC, sampling media, and expiration or lot requirements.
  2. Record the unique sample IDs before opening media. Confirm the pump, tubing, stand, charge, timing, and approved known-flow check.
  3. Place the sampler at the required location without disturbing dust or materials and use the current media-specific flow and duration.
  4. Cap and label the sample immediately, record location and collection conditions, and maintain required custody and transport conditions.
  5. Report deviations, equipment faults, disturbed media, or incomplete samples. Never change the plan merely to produce a result.

Source: MPI Mold / IAQ sampling field procedure and company pump guide.

What controls sampling flow and duration?

Built for the common field formats

Manufacturers have changed serial conventions over time. Each decoder is intentionally limited to the formats it can identify reliably.

Week + year

Carrier, ICP, Rheem, Trane, A. O. Smith

Converts production-week codes into an approximate calendar month, including supported 1960+ numeric codes.

Month + year

Goodman, Allied Air, Nortek, York, Rinnai

Reads numeric or letter month codes directly from the serial.

Special codes

Bradford White, Bosch, YORK commercial, Weil-McLain, Lochinvar, Navien, HTP, Ariston

Handles repeating letter cycles, factory date tables, CP ranges, legacy commercial formats, and an embedded product-date block.

Method, limitations, and reference notes

This is a field reference, not a warranty determination. Always compare the result with the printed manufacture date, model era, installation history, and manufacturer records—especially when a rating plate is damaged or a unit may be private-labeled.

1960 coverage does not mean every brand can be decoded to 1960. It applies only when the selected equipment uses one of the supported numeric date layouts. Repeating letter codes show every valid era instead of silently choosing one.
